propositions.text: The appeal is by the Information Commissioner from Federal Court decision dismissing judicial review of DND's 1,110-day extension under the Act.
propositions.quote: This is an appeal brought by the Information Commissioner of Canada (the Commissioner) from a decision of the Federal Court (2014 FC 205) wherein Kane J. (the Federal Court judge) dismissed her application for judicial review of a decision by the Department of National Defence (DND) to assert, in response to a request for records under the Access to Information Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. A-1 (the Act), an extension of 1,110 days.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal is from the Federal Court dismissing judicial review of DND's 1,110-day extension under the Act.

propositions.text: The Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario was granted leave to intervene in this appeal.
propositions.quote: The Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario (the intervener) was granted leave to intervene in the present appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario was allowed to intervene in the appeal.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Federal Court has jurisdiction under section 42 of the Act to review a government institution's subsection 9(1) extension decision.
propositions.quote: At issue is whether the Federal Court has jurisdiction under section 42 of the Act to review a decision by a government institution under subsection 9(1) to extend the time limit set out in section 7.

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge answered the jurisdiction question in the negative.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court judge answered this question in the negative.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is Federal Court jurisdiction under section 42 to review subsection 9(1) extensions; the Federal Court answered no.

propositions.text: The court proposes allowing the appeal for reasons that follow.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I would propose that the appeal be allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court proposes to allow the appeal for reasons explained later.

propositions.text: The relevant legislative provisions are set out in the annex to these reasons.
propositions.quote: The legislative provisions which are relevant to the analysis are set out in the annex to these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court states relevant legislative provisions are annexed to these reasons.

propositions.text: On February 3, 2011, a lawyer requested records from DND about military asset sales.
propositions.quote: On February 3, 2011, a lawyer acting for his clients (the requester) requested from DND access to records relating to the sale of certain military assets.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a lawyer requested military asset sale records from DND on February 3, 2011.

propositions.text: On March 4, 2011, DND extended the 30-day limit by 1,110 days under subsection 9(1).
propositions.quote: On March 4, 2011, DND notified the requester that, pursuant to subsection 9(1) of the Act, it was extending the 30-day time limit set out in section 7 by 1,110 days in order to deal with the request.

propositions.text: The requester communicated intent to file a complaint and did so on or about March 22, 2011.
propositions.quote: In response, the requester communicated his intent to file a complaint with the Commissioner and proceeded to do so on or about March 22, 2011.

paragraphs.summary: The court states DND extended the time limit by 1,110 days and the requester filed a complaint by March 22, 2011.

propositions.text: On March 29, 2011, the Commissioner notified intention to investigate under section 32 of the Act.
propositions.quote: On March 29, 2011, the Commissioner provided notice of her intention to investigate pursuant to section 32 of the Act.

propositions.text: DND informed the Commissioner that 230 days were under paragraph 9(1)(a) and 880 days under 9(1)(b).
propositions.quote: During the course of the investigation, DND informed the Commissioner that 230 of the 1,110 days had been taken under paragraph 9(1)(a) to deal with the large number of records involved and that the remaining 880 days had been taken under paragraph 9(1)(b) to complete the necessary consultations with third parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Commissioner began investigating and DND explained the extension days under paragraphs 9(1)(a) and (b).

propositions.text: In May 2012, DND identified 2,400 pages for review and cited reasons for the extension length.
propositions.quote: In May 2012, DND informed the Commissioner that it had identified 2,400 pages requiring review and consultation.

propositions.text: Reasons included solicitor-client privilege, software malfunction, and consultations with three government departments.
propositions.quote: DND also provided several reasons for the length of the extension taken, citing among other things the need to review the documents for matters of solicitor-client and litigation privilege, the occurrence of a major and unprecedented software malfunction in the department’s access to information unit, and the need to consult with three government departments, being Public Works and Government Services Canada (PWGSC), the Department of Justice (DOJ), and the Department of Foreign Affairs and International Trade (DFAIT).

propositions.text: DFAIT might need to consult with foreign governments.
propositions.quote: DND advised that DFAIT might in turn be required to consult with foreign governments.

paragraphs.summary: The court states DND identified 2,400 pages and cited privilege, software issues, and consultations including with DFAIT and foreign governments.

propositions.text: On July 9, 2012, DND sent records to three departments; PWGSC and DOJ responded by August 15, DFAIT responded August 31 needing 120 more days.
propositions.quote: On July 9, 2012, DND sent the relevant records to the three consulting departments. While PWGSC and DOJ provided a response to DND by August 15, 2012, DFAIT responded only on August 31, 2012, and notified DND that it would need another 120 days to complete its consultations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states DND sent records to three departments; DFAIT requested 120 more days after late response.

propositions.text: The Commissioner found DND breached subsection 4(2.1) by not making every effort to process timely.
propositions.quote: DND was found to have breached its duty under subsection 4(2.1) of the Act, as it failed to make every effort to process the request in a timely manner.

propositions.text: The extension was invalid: criteria under paragraph 9(1)(a) not met and 9(1)(b) time unreasonably long.
propositions.quote: DND’s asserted extension was also found to be invalid, as the criteria for an extension under paragraph 9(1)(a) were not all met, and the time taken under paragraph 9(1)(b) was unreasonably long.

propositions.text: The applicable time limit remained March 4, 2011; no response meant deemed refusal under subsection 10(3).
propositions.quote: Given the Commissioner’s finding of invalidity, she concluded that the applicable time limit for meeting the requester’s request remained March 4, 2011, 30 days past the point in time at which the original request had been made. Because no response had been received by that date, DND was found to have been in a state of deemed refusal pursuant to subsection 10(3) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner found DND breached duty, extension invalid, and DND deemed to have refused by March 4, 2011.

propositions.text: The Commissioner recommended DND respond by February 28, 2013.
propositions.quote: The Commissioner recommended that DND commit to respond by February 28, 2013.

propositions.text: On November 6, 2012, DND said it could not commit due to external consultations beyond its control.
propositions.quote: On November 6, 2012, DND informed the Commissioner that it could not so commit, as the consultations in question were external and beyond its control.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner recommended a response deadline; DND declined due to external consultations.

propositions.text: On January 11, 2013, the Commissioner filed judicial review application seeking declaration of deemed refusal and order to respond within 30 days.
propositions.quote: On January 11, 2013, acting under section 42 of the Act, the Commissioner filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court. The Commissioner sought a declaration that DND was in a state of deemed refusal for having failed to give access within the time limits set out in the Act and an order directing DND to respond to the request within a 30-day period.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Commissioner filed judicial review seeking declaration of deemed refusal and order to respond within 30 days.

propositions.text: On September 11, 2013, DND gave requester access 27 days before hearing.
propositions.quote: On September 11, 2013, 27 days before the Federal Court hearing, DND gave the requester access to the requested documents.

propositions.text: DND moved to dismiss the application as moot due to access being given.
propositions.quote: Given this development, DND moved to dismiss the Commissioner’s application on the basis that the underlying issue had become moot.

paragraphs.summary: The court states DND gave access before hearing and moved to dismiss application as moot.

propositions.text: The motion to dismiss was heard on October 8, 2013, with the judicial review application.
propositions.quote: The motion to dismiss was heard on October 8, 2013, in conjunction with the judicial review application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the motion to dismiss was heard with the judicial review application on October 8, 2013.

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge found the dispute moot but exercised discretion to consider the declaration request.
propositions.quote: Though she agreed that the dispute was moot, consideration of the factors set out in Borowski v. Canada (Attorney General), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342, 57 D.L.R. (4th) 231 led her to exercise her discretion to nevertheless consider the Commissioner’s request for a declaration.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found the dispute moot but chose to consider the declaration request.

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge first considered whether the Federal Court had jurisdiction under section 42 to issue the declaration.
propositions.quote: Before considering the reasonableness of the extension taken by DND, the Federal court judge first considered whether the Federal Court had jurisdiction pursuant to section 42 of the Act to issue the requested declaration.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge first considered Federal Court jurisdiction under section 42 to issue the declaration.

propositions.text: The jurisdiction question turned on whether a subsection 9(1) extension can amount to deemed refusal under subsection 10(3).
propositions.quote: According to the Federal Court judge, the answer to this question turned on whether and when a time extension taken by a government institution pursuant to subsection 9(1) of the Act can amount to a deemed refusal under subsection 10(3).

propositions.text: Federal Court jurisdiction is limited to refusals; deemed refusal is the only way to challenge extensions without outright refusal.
propositions.quote: Because the Federal Court’s jurisdiction is limited to instances of refusal (sections 41 and 42), a deemed refusal is the only route by which to challenge a government institution which extends the time under subsection 9(1), without actually refusing to provide the requested records.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found jurisdiction depends on whether subsection 9(1) extensions can be deemed refusals under subsection 10(3).

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge concluded deemed refusal occurs only if access is not given by the extension expiry date.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court judge ultimately concluded that, where a government institution takes an extension under subsection 9(1), it will not enter a state of deemed refusal unless and until it fails to give access by the date on which the asserted extension expires (Reasons at paras. 97 to 99).

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge concluded deemed refusal arises only if access is not given by the extension expiry date.

propositions.text: The Federal Court judge supported her conclusion by analyzing the Act's language on time limits and deemed refusal.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court judge supported this conclusion on several grounds. First, she pointed to the language of the Act. Under section 7 of the Act, the head of a government institution has 30 days to respond to an access request. Subsection 9(1) of the Act allows for the extension of this 30-day limit “for a reasonable period of time, having regard to the circumstances”. Subsection 10(3) of the Act deems a refusal to have taken place where the records requested are not provided within the time limits provided by the Act. According to the Federal Court judge, this last provision provides in effect that “where there is no outright refusal of access, if the requested records are not provided within 30 days or within the period of time claimed as an extension under section 9, there is a deemed refusal” (Reasons at para. 66).

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge reasoned the Act's language means deemed refusal occurs if records are not provided within 30 days or the extension period.

propositions.text: Section 30 distinguishes complaints after refusals and extensions, but sections 41 and 42 only mention refusals for judicial review
propositions.quote: Section 30, in setting out when the Commissioner shall investigate complaints, distinguishes between complaints following a refusal of access (paragraph 30(1)(a)) and those following an asserted extension that the requester believes to be unreasonable (paragraph 30(1)(c)). Sections 41 and 42, however, in setting out the grounds for judicial review, speak only of refusals.

propositions.text: Parliament would have expressly granted Federal Court jurisdiction to review extensions if intended, as it did for complaints to the Commissioner
propositions.quote: Had Parliament intended to grant the Federal Court jurisdiction to review the reasonableness of extensions, it would have done so expressly, as it did in setting out the grounds for complaints to the Commissioner (Reasons at paras. 96, 105 and 106).

propositions.text: Only remedy for unreasonable extension is Commissioner's investigation and recommendations, not judicial review
propositions.quote: Read together, the provisions make it clear that, ultimately, the only remedy available for an allegedly unreasonable extension is to invite the Commissioner to investigate, make recommendations to the government institution concerned and, if necessary, make note of the behaviour in her Annual or Special Report (Reasons at paras. 105 and 109).

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found sections 41 and 42 limit judicial review to refusals, not extensions, and only the Commissioner can investigate extensions.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge relied on PSAC decision holding no refusal or review under section 41 until request deadline passes
propositions.quote: She relied in particular on Public Service Alliance of Canada v. Canada (Attorney General), 2011 FC 649, 391 F.T.R. 28 [PSAC] wherein Beaudry J. stated (at para. 21): In my view, there can be no refusal and therefore no review pursuant to section 41 of the Act until the deadline for processing a request has passed.

propositions.text: PSAC decision limits court jurisdiction to review refusals, excluding extensions
propositions.quote: The language of the Act clearly limits this Court’s jurisdiction to the review of refusals, whether actual or deemed, and leaves no room for the review of extensions.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge relied on PSAC to find no judicial review under section 41 until request deadline passes, excluding extensions.

propositions.text: In Attorney General decision, no deemed refusal exists if extended time limit not yet passed
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the time limit for giving access has been extended to three years and that time period has not yet passed. Accordingly, there is no “deemed refusal to give access” since the government institution has not refused to give access within the extended time limit.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge cited Attorney General decision holding no deemed refusal if extended time limit not passed.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge noted two other decisions favoring judicial review of extensions but found jurisprudence consistent
propositions.quote: The Federal Court judge took note of two other Federal Court decisions which, according to the Commissioner, went the other way (Reasons at para. 89, citing Canada (Information Commissioner) v. Canada (Minister of External Affairs), [1989] 1 F.C. 3 (T.D.) [External Affairs(I)] and Canada (Information Commissioner) v. Canada (Minister of External Affairs), [1990] 3 F.C. 514, 3 T.C.T. 5297 [External Affairs(II)]), but held nevertheless that the jurisprudence has not been shown to be inconsistent (Reasons at para. 101).

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge acknowledged contrary decisions but found the case law consistent.

propositions.text: Policy reasons support limiting judicial review of extensions to avoid inefficiency and resource duplication
propositions.quote: If the Commissioner’s position were accepted, the asserted extension would have been held to be invalid and DND would therefore have been deemed to have refused access following the expiry of the 30-day time limit provided for under section 7 of the Act. In the Federal Court judge’s view, such a decision would not necessarily have sped up the provision of the requested records in the case at bar (Reasons at para. 112). Moreover, the Court might not be best positioned to determine what the appropriate time to comply would be (ibidem). Finally, DND would be required to respond at once to both the judicial review application and the access request, potentially “duplicat[ing] efforts and spread[ing] resources even thinner” (ibidem).

propositions.text: Government institutions needing to meet 30-day limit without extensions require more resources
propositions.quote: According to the Federal Court judge, if government institutions are to make the 30-day time limit without extensions, they will simply need greater resources (Reasons at paras. 126 to 127).

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found policy reasons against judicial review of extensions and said institutions need more resources to meet deadlines.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge held no jurisdiction to issue declaration as DND met its own extension deadlines
propositions.quote: As DND provided access to the documents claimed within its own deadlines as asserted under subsection 9(1), the Federal Court judge held that she had no jurisdiction to issue the declaration sought.

propositions.text: No need to decide reasonableness of 1,110-day extension since no jurisdiction to issue declaration
propositions.quote: Hence, there was no need for the Court to decide whether the 1,110-day extension was reasonable (Reasons at para. 122).

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge held no jurisdiction to declare on extension reasonableness as DND met its deadlines.

propositions.text: Extension under section 9 is conditional exception to 30-day limit; invalid if conditions unmet
propositions.quote: The Commissioner argues that an extension under section 9 of the Act represents a conditional exception to the 30-day time limit set out in section 7 (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 42, 45, and 51). Where a government institution asserts an extension under section 9, but fails to meet the conditions, the extension is void ab initio (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 63).

propositions.text: One condition is that extension be reasonable given circumstances
propositions.quote: One of the conditions under section 9 is that the extension be for “a reasonable period of time, having regard to the circumstances” (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 42, 45, and 51).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues section 9 extensions are conditional and void if unreasonable or conditions unmet.

propositions.text: Deemed refusal occurs if no access or refusal within Act's time limits including extensions
propositions.quote: Subsection 10(3) provides that a deemed refusal occurs where a government institution fails to give access to a requested record “within the time limits set out in [the] Act”. Read together, sections 7 and 9 set out these time limits (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 61). A deemed refusal will therefore occur after 30 days if a government institution has given neither an actual refusal nor access in response to a request and has taken no valid extension (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 49 and 63).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues deemed refusal arises if no valid extension and no access or refusal within time limits.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge erred by ignoring cases showing broad construction of sections 41 and 42 for judicial review
propositions.quote: The Commissioner argues that the Federal Court judge erred in her comparison of section 30 to sections 41 and 42. Specifically, she ignored several cases which show that these latter sections are to be broadly construed, and contemplate grounds of judicial review not expressly set out in their language (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 67 to 68, citing Clearwater v. Canada (Minister of Canadian Heritage), 177 F.T.R. 103 (F.C.), [1999] F.C.J. No. 1441 and Canada (Information Commissioner) v. Canada (Minister of National Defence), [1990] 3 F.C. 22 (T.D), [1990] F.C.J. No. 152).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues the Federal Court judge wrongly ignored cases supporting broad judicial review under sections 41 and 42.

propositions.text: Judge's interpretation conflicts with Act's principle of independent review of government disclosure decisions
propositions.quote: The Commissioner further submits that the Federal Court judge’s interpretation conflicts with the principle, enshrined in section 2 of the Act, that “decisions on the disclosure of government information should be reviewed independently of government” (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 69, citing section 2 of the Act).

propositions.text: Allowing judge's view would let government institutions avoid judicial review
propositions.quote: The decision of the Federal Court judge would, if allowed to stand, permit government institutions to immunize themselves from judicial review (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 72).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues the judge's view conflicts with independent review and would let government avoid judicial review.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge erred in assessing earlier decisions as they involved different facts and pre-amendment law
propositions.quote: The Commissioner argues that the Federal Court judge erred in her assessment of earlier Federal Court decisions. The Commissioner maintains that PSAC and Attorney General dealt with an entirely different set of facts (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 78). Moreover, Attorney General was decided before subsection 4(2.1) was added to the Act in 2006, and the judge deciding PSAC did not consider this amendment, which requires government institutions to assist requesters and provide timely access to sought records (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 80).

propositions.text: Judge failed to address External Affairs(I) statement that courts must review extensions to determine deemed refusal
propositions.quote: Finally, the Commissioner argues that the Federal Court judge erred in failing to confront the statement made in External Affairs(I) to the effect that (per Jerome A.C.J. at para. 19): … (w)here the application is based on an allegedly unauthorized extension taken under section 9, that enquiry consists of determining … whether it amounts to a deemed refusal. To perform that task, it is inescapable that the Court must be able to review the extension itself and reasons given therefor.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues the judge erred by misapplying earlier decisions and ignoring External Affairs(I) requiring court review of extensions.

propositions.text: Judge wrongly suggested courts not well-placed to determine reasonableness of extensions
propositions.quote: The Commissioner also takes issue with the Federal Court judge’s suggestion that the Court may not be well-placed to determine whether an extension of time is reasonable.

propositions.text: Act empowers Commissioner to investigate extensions and courts apply deferential reasonableness standard
propositions.quote: The Act empowers the Commissioner to investigate extensions of time and assemble a factual record that may be brought before the Federal Court for adjudication (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 84 and 88). Concerns that the courts should avoid “second-guessing” government institutions evince a concern that the courts will micro-manage extensions. This concern can be seen to be misplaced given the deferential standard to be applied (i.e. reasonableness) (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 91).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues courts are well-placed to review extensions using a deferential reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Court should exercise discretion to rule on invalid extension for efficiency as record is written
propositions.quote: In this instance, the Commissioner says, the asserted extension was invalid and, for purposes of efficiency, this Court should exercise its discretion to rule on the matter. Because the evidentiary record is in writing, this Court is in no worse a position than the court below to decide this question.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner urges this Court to rule on the invalid extension for efficiency since the record is written.

propositions.text: 230-day extension under paragraph 9(1)(a) was invalid as DND failed to show unreasonable interference with operations
propositions.quote: First, it claims that the 230-day portion of the extension taken pursuant to paragraph 9(1)(a) was not taken in compliance with the statutory conditions, as DND could not show, as required by the provision in question, that meeting the request within the 30-day time limit would unreasonably interfere with its operations (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 96 to 98).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner claims the 230-day extension was invalid as DND failed to prove unreasonable interference with operations.

propositions.text: 880-day extension under paragraph 9(1)(b) was unreasonably long and based on flawed calculation
propositions.quote: Second, the Commissioner claims that the remaining period, being the 880 days asserted pursuant to paragraph 9(1)(b), was unreasonably long. DND’s initial explanation was that it had merely calculated the average DFAIT response time (110 days) and multiplied it by eight, because the requester had sought approximately eight times the number of records typically sent to DFAIT for consultation (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 102).

propositions.text: DND could not explain why estimate remained 880 days despite later amendments
propositions.quote: Though DND later amended its answer to suggest that such factors were accounted for, it could not explain why the number had then remained exactly 880 days (Commissioner’s memorandum at para. 104).

propositions.text: Actual consultations took only 173 days, supporting unreasonableness of 880-day estimate
propositions.quote: That the actual consultations took no longer than 173 days further supports the unreasonableness of this estimate (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 105 and 106).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner argues the 880-day extension was unreasonably long, based on flawed calculation, and actual consultations took only 173 days.

propositions.text: DND unreasonably exercised discretion by ignoring duty to assist and relevant policies
propositions.quote: Third, the Commissioner claims generally that DND exercised its discretion unreasonably in asserting the extension it did. First, it failed to consider such relevant factors as its duty to assist under subsection 4(2.1) of the Act, the quasi-constitutional status of the Act, and relevant government policies (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 108 to 110, citing Treasury Board of Canada, Policy on Access to Information, sections 3.1, 6.2.1 and 6.2.2).

propositions.text: DND considered irrelevant factors and abdicated responsibility by blaming other institutions
propositions.quote: Second, it considered irrelevant factors such as potential causes of delay and abdicated all responsibility by asserting that it had no control over the responses of other institutions (Commissioner’s memorandum at paras. 111 to 113).

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner claims DND unreasonably exercised discretion by ignoring duties and blaming others for delays.

propositions.text: Intervener shows Ontario courts find reasonableness of extensions justiciable and lists evidentiary factors
propositions.quote: In his submissions, the intervener undertook to illustrate that, in Ontario, the reasonableness of an extension to respond to an access to information request has proven to be a justiciable question (Intervener’s memorandum at para. 35). In support of this effort, the intervener canvassed the evidentiary factors considered in determining whether a government institution has proven its claim that a given extension was required for the reasons set out in the intervener’s enabling statute (Intervener’s memorandum at paras. 22 to 25).

paragraphs.summary: The intervener argues Ontario courts consider reasonableness of extensions justiciable and lists evidentiary factors.

propositions.text: Intervener questions validity of DND's formula for 880-day extension and notes Ontario limits extensions to 10 months
propositions.quote: Though the intervener took no formal position on the disposition of the case at bar, he took issue with the duration of the extension claimed. In particular, he questioned the validity of the formula originally offered by DND in support of the 880-day portion of the extension taken (Intervener’s memorandum at paras. 9 and 23). More generally, the intervener noted that, in the Ontario setting, no extension exceeding 10 months has ever been found to be reasonable (Intervener’s memorandum at para. 25).

paragraphs.summary: The intervener questions DND's 880-day extension formula and notes Ontario courts never find extensions over 10 months reasonable.

propositions.text: DND argues Federal Court judge correctly construed Act and case law for reasons given
propositions.quote: DND argues that the Federal Court judge correctly construed the Act and properly assessed the case law, essentially for the reasons that she gave. Significant sections of the written submissions repeat the judge’s own language (see for instance DND’s memorandum at paras. 35 and 70).

paragraphs.summary: DND supports the Federal Court judge's interpretation and reasoning as correct.

propositions.text: DND argues government was unwilling to impose definitive time limits for extensions under section 9
propositions.quote: DND argues that, in reviewing the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, it can be seen that the government was not prepared to impose a definitive time limit for extensions under subsection 9(1) of the Act (DND’s memorandum at para. 47).

propositions.text: If Parliament intended court review of extensions, it would have used more specific language than 'reasonable... having regard to the circumstances'
propositions.quote: Furthermore, if Parliament had intended the Federal Court to have the jurisdiction to review extensions, it would have used more specific language rather than simply requiring that extensions be “reasonable … having regard to the circumstances” (DND’s memorandum at para. 48).

propositions.text: If deemed refusals included unreasonable or excessive extensions, Parliament would have specified this
propositions.quote: Finally, if Parliament had intended for deemed refusals under subsection 10(3) of the Act to include instances in which the government institution takes an unreasonable extension under section 9 or an extension beyond a defined length, it could have specified this (DND’s memorandum at para. 49).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues Parliament did not intend definitive extension limits or judicial review of extensions under the Act.

propositions.text: DND argues sections 41 and 42 limit complaints to refusals, excluding unreasonable extensions from Federal Court jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: DND reiterates its argument, accepted by the Federal Court judge, that while the paragraphs of subsection 30(1) of the Act clearly distinguish between refusals and unreasonable extensions in setting out the grounds of complaint to the Commissioner, sections 41 and 42 are limited to refusals (DND’s memorandum at paras. 51 to 52).

propositions.text: DND argues Parliament could have included judicial review for extensions but did not, unlike in complaint provisions.
propositions.quote: Had Parliament wished to grant the Federal Court jurisdiction to decide the reasonableness of extensions, it could have included in the judicial review section of the Act a provision like the one included in the complaint section (DND’s memorandum at para. 52).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues sections 41 and 42 limit complaints to refusals, excluding extensions, and Parliament could have included judicial review for extensions but did not.

propositions.text: DND argues the Commissioner has only an ombudsman role without power to compel compliance, so findings are not judicially reviewable decisions.
propositions.quote: DND further argues that, contrary to some equivalent provincial statutory schemes, Parliament expressly limited the Commissioner to an ombudsman role, declining to vest her with the powers to compel compliance with the Act (DND’s memorandum at para. 55). The Commissioner’s findings are therefore not “decisions” that may be judicially reviewed.

propositions.text: DND argues the Commissioner cannot initiate judicial review upon finding an unreasonable extension.
propositions.quote: This undermines the Commissioner’s argument that, the moment she finds that an unreasonable extension has been asserted, she may initiate a judicial review application (DND’s memorandum at para. 56).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues the Commissioner is only an ombudsman without power to compel, so findings are not reviewable and cannot trigger judicial review.

propositions.text: DND argues the Federal Court ruling aligns with the principle that not all decisions under the Act require judicial review.
propositions.quote: Finally, DND argues that the Federal Court judge’s ruling is not inconsistent with the section 2 principle that decisions on the disclosure of government information should be reviewed independently of government. Simply put, this principle does not require that all decisions made under the Act be subject to judicial review (DND’s memorandum at para. 58).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues the Federal Court ruling aligns with the principle that not all decisions under the Act require judicial review.

propositions.text: DND argues that if the Court has jurisdiction, its extension was reasonable.
propositions.quote: In the event that this Court finds that it does have jurisdiction to issue the declaration sought, DND argues that its extension was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: DND argues that if the Court has jurisdiction, its extension was reasonable.

propositions.text: DND argues its only obligation under subsection 9(1) was to notify the requester of the extension and its length.
propositions.quote: DND insists that its only obligation under subsection 9(1) was to notify the requester that it would be taking an extension and to specify the length of the extension (DND’s memorandum at para. 61).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues its only obligation under subsection 9(1) was to notify the requester of the extension and its length.

propositions.text: DND argues it considered variables like past experience, sensitivity, and workload in determining extension length.
propositions.quote: DND argues that many variables were taken into account in determining the amount of time it took under paragraph 9(1)(a) of the Act, including previous experience with similar requests, sensitivity of the information and the current workload of the analyst assigned to the file (DND’s memorandum at para. 63).

propositions.text: DND's access to information unit had a major software malfunction affecting response time.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, DND’s access to information unit had suffered a “major and unprecedented” software malfunction, which further affected the response time (ibidem).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues it considered variables and a major software malfunction affected response time in determining extension length.

propositions.text: DND argues it considered past experience and communication in consultations, especially unpredictable foreign government reactions.
propositions.quote: As to consultations, DND argues that previous experience and communication with the other institutions was taken into account (DND’s memorandum at para. 64). Estimates were particularly difficult to generate in respect of the DFAIT consultations, as the reactions of foreign governments often prove difficult to predict accurately (DND’s memorandum at paras. 65 to 67).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues it considered past experience and communication in consultations, especially unpredictable foreign government reactions.

propositions.text: DND argues it has only 30 days to determine extension length and cannot change it later, so considering delay causes is reasonable.
propositions.quote: DND emphasized that, under subsection 9(1) of the Act, it only has 30 days to determine the extension it will take (DND’s memorandum at para. 68). Furthermore, it cannot change that estimate. It is therefore reasonable to consider potential causes of delay (ibidem).

propositions.text: DND argues that actual shorter consultation time is irrelevant to reasonableness of extension at assertion time.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, that the consultations ultimately took less time than expected is irrelevant to whether, at the time the extension was asserted, the duration selected was reasonable (DND’s memorandum at para. 69).

paragraphs.summary: DND argues it has 30 days to determine extension and cannot change it; actual shorter consultation time is irrelevant to reasonableness.

propositions.text: DND distinguishes the Act from Ontario's FOI Act, noting federal Commissioner has investigative, not adjudicative, role.
propositions.quote: In reply to the submissions made by the intervener, DND outlined the differences between the Act and the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.31, emphasizing that the latter gives the provincial Commissioner an adjudicative role, while the former gives the federal Commissioner an investigative one (Respondent’s reply memorandum at paras. 15 to 18).

propositions.text: DND submits intervener lacks expertise in cases involving military assets and foreign government consultations.
propositions.quote: With respect to the intervener’s view that extensions beyond 10 months would require an exceptional justification, DND submits that the intervener has no expertise or experience in cases such as this one, which involves military assets and consultation with foreign governments (Respondent’s reply memorandum at paras. 25 and 26).

paragraphs.summary: DND distinguishes federal Commissioner’s investigative role from provincial adjudicative role and says intervener lacks expertise in military and foreign consultation cases.

propositions.text: This Court is determining an appeal of the Federal Court's dismissal of the Commissioner's judicial review application under paragraph 42(1)(a).
propositions.quote: In this case, this Court is determining an appeal of a decision by the Federal Court to dismiss an application for judicial review brought by the Commissioner under paragraph 42(1)(a).

paragraphs.summary: This Court is determining an appeal of the Federal Court's dismissal of the Commissioner's judicial review application under paragraph 42(1)(a).

propositions.text: The appeal raises two issues: Federal Court's jurisdiction under section 42 and validity of DND's extension if jurisdiction exists.
propositions.quote: The appeal raises two issues. The first is whether the Federal Court had jurisdiction under section 42 of the Act to hear the Commissioner’s application. The second, which must be answered only if the first question is answered in the affirmative, is whether the extension taken by DND was valid.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal raises two issues: Federal Court's jurisdiction under section 42 and validity of DND's extension if jurisdiction exists.

propositions.text: The first issue is preliminary and decided by Federal Court; appellate standard of review applies, not administrative.
propositions.quote: The first issue is preliminary to any consideration of the underlying application, concerning whether the preconditions for a judicial review are met. As such, this question was first decided by the Federal Court, and never arose before the administrative decision-maker in question. Therefore, on appeal, we employ the appellate standard of review in Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 [Housen], not the administrative standard of review in Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190.

paragraphs.summary: The first issue is preliminary and decided by Federal Court; appellate standard of review applies, not administrative.

propositions.text: Whether judicial review preconditions are met depends on statutory construction of sections 41, 42, 7, 9(1), and 10(3).
propositions.quote: Whether the preconditions for a judicial review had been met turns on a pure question of statutory construction, i.e. when an extension is taken by a government institution, does the Act (specifically sections 41 and 42 when read with section 7 and subsections 9(1) and 10(3)) give the Federal Court jurisdiction to assess the legal validity of the extension?

propositions.text: Federal Court answered no to jurisdiction to assess extension validity.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court answered this in the negative.

propositions.text: Determination on question of law reviewed on correctness standard per Housen.
propositions.quote: As a determination on a question of law, this holding stands within the appellate framework to be reviewed on the standard of correctness: Housen, supra at paras. 8 and 9.

paragraphs.summary: Whether judicial review preconditions are met depends on statutory construction; Federal Court said no jurisdiction; correctness standard applies.

propositions.text: If section 42 preconditions met, Court must review validity of DND's extension on appropriate standard of review.
propositions.quote: If I hold that the section 42 preconditions have been met in this case, I must examine whether the extension taken by DND in this case was valid. The Federal Court judge did not rule on that question. Therefore, consistent with the approach set out in Agraira v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36, [2013] 2 S.C.R. 559 at paragraphs 45 to 47, I must select the appropriate standard of review and then apply it myself.

paragraphs.summary: If section 42 preconditions met, Court must review validity of DND's extension on appropriate standard of review.

propositions.text: Validity of extension reviewed on reasonableness standard with broad margin of appreciation for DND.
propositions.quote: Like the parties, I accept that this second question should be reviewed on a standard of reasonableness. I would add that, because the decision under review is essentially fact and policy driven, the range of possible acceptable outcomes or the margin of appreciation to be given to DND is broad: Canada (Minister of Transport, Infrastructure and Communities) v. Jagjit Singh Farwaha, 2014 FCA 56 at paras. 91 to 92; Canada (Attorney General) v. Abraham, 2012 FCA 266, [2012] F.C.J. No. 1324 at para.

paragraphs.summary: Validity of extension reviewed on reasonableness standard with broad margin of appreciation for DND.

propositions.text: Federal Court held subsection 10(3) deems refusal if records not provided within time limits, so no judicial review if extension complied with.
propositions.quote: … subsection 10(3) provides that where the records are not provided within the time limits set out in this act, the head of the institution is deemed to have refused to give access. In other words, where there is no outright notice of refusal, if the requested records are not provided within 30 days or within the period of time claimed as an extension under section 9, there is a deemed refusal. Stated conversely and perhaps more accurately, the Federal Court judge held that so long as there is compliance with the time extension taken, there can be no deemed refusal pursuant to subsection 10(3) regardless of the reasonableness of the extension, and therefore no right of judicial review arises in the circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court held subsection 10(3) deems refusal if records not provided within time limits, so no judicial review if extension complied with.

propositions.text: Federal Court's reading aligns with some Federal Court decisions but conflicts with others.
propositions.quote: As will be seen, the reading proposed by the Federal Court judge is consistent with a number of Federal Court decisions (X v. Canada (Minister of National Defence), [1991] 1 F.C. 670, 41 F.T.R. 73 at paras. 8 and 10 [X]; Attorney General at paras. 25 to 27, citing X at para. 8; PSAC at para. 21, citing Attorney General at para. 25). There are, however, other cases from the same court which go the other way (External Affairs(I) at para. 19 and External Affairs(II) at para. 9).

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court's reading aligns with some Federal Court decisions but conflicts with others.

propositions.text: Statutory interpretation requires reading words in context, harmoniously with Act's scheme, object, and Parliament's intent.
propositions.quote: The correct approach to statutory interpretation requires that courts read “the words of an Act … in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament” (Thibodeau v. Air Canada, 2014 SCC 67, [2014] S.C.J. No. 67 at para. 112).

paragraphs.summary: Statutory interpretation requires reading words in context, harmoniously with Act's scheme, object, and Parliament's intent.

propositions.text: Federal Court's interpretation lets government institutions set extension length without judicial review, contrary to statutory scheme.
propositions.quote: Based on the Federal Court judge’s interpretation, the length of this last time limit would rest exclusively in the hands of the government institution asserting it, and escape judicial review regardless of its duration.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court's interpretation lets government institutions set extension length without judicial review, contrary to statutory scheme.

propositions.text: Interpreting subsection 9(1) as allowing unlimited extension time ignores the reasonableness requirement and negates 'time limits' concept.
propositions.quote: For the purpose of applying subsection 10(3), construing subsection 9(1) as allowing for whatever period of time the institution may wish to take reads out of the Act the requirement that the extension be “reasonable … having regard to the circumstances” and the criteria set out in paragraphs 9(1)(a) and 9(1)(b).

propositions.text: The extended 'time limit' accepted by Federal Court is not a true limit if institution can choose any deadline.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the extended “time limit” that the Federal Court judge accepts as falling within the “time limits set out in [the] Act” (Reasons at para. 66) is not a time limit at all. If a government institution is free to choose the deadline of its choice, without regard to the statutory conditions set out in subsection 9(1), there are no limits on the deadline it may choose.

paragraphs.summary: Interpreting subsection 9(1) as allowing unlimited extension time ignores reasonableness and negates 'time limits' concept; extended limit is not a true limit.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge compared section 30 to sections 41 and 42 and found no express judicial review for unreasonable time limits
propositions.quote: The Federal Court judge’s interpretation is not aided by her comparison of section 30 of the Act to sections 41 and 42. According to her, had Parliament intended unreasonable time limits to be judicially reviewed, it would have set this out expressly

propositions.text: If unreasonable extensions could cause deemed refusals under subsection 10(3), paragraph 30(1)(c) would be unnecessary
propositions.quote: if unreasonable extensions could give rise to deemed refusals pursuant to subsection 10(3) as the Commissioner contends, there would be no need for paragraph 30(1)(c)

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found no express judicial review for unreasonable time limits and argued paragraph 30(1)(c) would be unnecessary if unreasonable extensions caused deemed refusals.

propositions.text: Subsection 10(3) clearly states deemed refusal occurs if time limits in the Act are missed, so inferences are unhelpful
propositions.quote: subsection 10(3) makes it clear that a deemed refusal occurs where a government institution has missed either of “the time limits set out in [the] Act”

propositions.text: Using inferences to interpret deemed refusal for sections 41 and 42 is problematic and differs from the Act's express wording
propositions.quote: it is therefore not useful to resort to inferences to elucidate the meaning of a deemed refusal for purposes of applying sections 41 and 42 and particularly problematic when, as here, doing so would lead to a meaning that is different from what is expressly stated in the Act

paragraphs.summary: The court finds subsection 10(3) clearly defines deemed refusal and rejects inferring meanings differing from the Act's express wording.

propositions.text: Paragraph 30(1)(c) allows immediate Commissioner assistance if requester receives extension notice within 30 days
propositions.quote: paragraph 30(1)(c) provides a requester with the same immediate right to invoke the assistance of the Commissioner as he or she would have if confronted with an outright refusal

propositions.text: Timely access is a key part of the right of access under subsection 4(2.1) of the Act
propositions.quote: timely access is a constituent part of the right of access (see subsection 4(2.1) of the Act)

paragraphs.summary: The court finds paragraph 30(1)(c) grants immediate Commissioner assistance upon extension notice and timely access is a key right.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge concluded no inconsistency in jurisprudence, but two decisions hold extensions must be judicially reviewed
propositions.quote: The Federal Court judge’s conclusion that “there is no footing to argue that the jurisprudence is inconsistent” is unexplained

propositions.text: External Affairs(I) and (II) hold courts must review extensions and require cogent reasons for them
propositions.quote: External Affairs(I)¸ Jerome A.C.J. held that... the court is required to review the extension itself and decide whether it was justified... External Affairs(II), Muldoon J. came to the same conclusion

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found no jurisprudence inconsistency, but two decisions require courts to review and justify extensions.

propositions.text: Federal Court judge adopted PSAC reasoning rejecting External Affairs decisions but gave no more precedential value
propositions.quote: the Federal Court judge adopts the reasoning of Beaudry J. in PSAC... his decision has no more precedential value than the other two

propositions.text: Federal Court judge may adopt one position over another if reasons are explained (Apotex cases)
propositions.quote: It was of course open to the Federal Court judge to adopt one position and reject the other, subject to explaining her reasons for doing so

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge adopted PSAC reasoning rejecting External Affairs but must explain reasons when choosing positions.

propositions.text: PSAC reasoning is flawed as it ignores subsection 9(1) conditions for valid extensions
propositions.quote: PSAC ought not to be followed because the reasoning advanced in that case does not confront or take into account the requirement that a valid extension must comply with the statutory conditions set out in subsection 9(1)

propositions.text: Same flaw applies to X and Attorney General cases
propositions.quote: The same observation extends to X and Attorney General

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PSAC and similar cases flawed for ignoring subsection 9(1) conditions for valid extensions.

propositions.text: DND's argument that Parliament would specify time limits if judicial review intended is rejected
propositions.quote: I do not accept DND’s attempts to support the interpretation of the Federal Court judge on other grounds. Specifically, it does not follow that specific time limits defined in days would have been set out in the Act had Parliament intended that extensions be judicially reviewed

propositions.text: Reasonableness in subsection 9(1) is a core legal standard appropriate for assessing extensions
propositions.quote: The concept of “reasonableness” embodied in subsection 9(1) is a core legal standard which courts are regularly called upon to apply

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects DND's argument and affirms reasonableness as a core legal standard for assessing extensions.

propositions.text: DND relies on Standing Committee minutes suggesting difficulty setting firm time limits
propositions.quote: Similarly, the excerpts relied upon by DND from the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs are of no assistance

propositions.text: The committee noted difficulty setting definitive time limits due to volume and complexity of requests
propositions.quote: I find it rather difficult to set a definitive period of time within which the head of the institution must give access to the record... it is rather difficult to give the undertaking that the answer must be given within a certain period of time

paragraphs.summary: DND relies on committee minutes noting difficulty setting firm time limits; court finds this does not assist DND's position.

propositions.text: Committee minutes do not suggest Federal Court lacks jurisdiction over extensions under section 9
propositions.quote: I do not read this passage as suggesting that the Federal Court was to have no jurisdiction over the extensions taken under section 9

propositions.text: The minutes reject only a firm 30-day cap on extensions, not judicial review
propositions.quote: the only proposition being rejected is the one which prompted this response, i.e. limiting the extensions permissible by applying a firm 30-day cap

paragraphs.summary: The court finds committee minutes reject a firm 30-day cap but do not deny Federal Court jurisdiction over extensions.

propositions.text: DND argues Commissioner's investigative findings are not judicially reviewable, barring review of extensions
propositions.quote: the fact that the Commissioner’s investigative findings made pursuant to subsection 37(1) are not subject to judicial review cannot be set up as a bar against the Commissioner’s entitlement to bring an application for judicial review

propositions.text: Decision under review is the institution's extension decision, not Commissioner's findings, so judicial review is possible
propositions.quote: the decision under review is the one taken by the government institution to extend the time limit, not the findings made by the Commissioner in respect of that decision

propositions.text: It is difficult to imagine Commissioner making a decision and then seeking its judicial review
propositions.quote: Indeed, it is difficult to visualize a scheme whereby the Commissioner would make a decision and then seek its judicial review

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects DND's argument, holding judicial review targets institution's extension decision, not Commissioner's findings.

propositions.text: Section 7 requires government institutions to respond within 30 days, subject to exceptions including section 9 extensions
propositions.quote: Section 7 of the Act requires a government institution to respond to an information request within 30 days. This requirement is subject to several exceptions, one of which is the power... to extend the time

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 7 requires responses within 30 days, subject to exceptions like section 9 extensions.

propositions.text: Extensions under section 9 must be reasonable per subsection 9(1) conditions or else 30-day limit remains
propositions.quote: A government institution may avail itself of this power subject to certain conditions... If this condition is not satisfied, the time is not validly extended with the result that the 30-day time limit imposed by operation of section 7 remains the applicable limit

paragraphs.summary: The court holds extensions must meet subsection 9(1) reasonableness conditions or the 30-day limit applies.

propositions.text: Deemed refusal arises if 30-day limit expires without access and no valid extension taken
propositions.quote: a deemed refusal arises whenever the initial 30-day time limit has expired without access being given, in circumstances where no legally valid extension has been taken

propositions.text: Right to judicially review extension validity arises under sections 41 and/or 42 after 30-day limit expires
propositions.quote: a right to judicially review the validity of an extension arises pursuant to sections 41 and/or 42 upon the expiration of the 30-day time limit

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes deemed refusal occurs without valid extension after 30 days, triggering judicial review rights under sections 41/42.

propositions.text: Federal Court had jurisdiction to review DND's extension and consider its validity
propositions.quote: I conclude that the Federal Court had the jurisdiction to entertain the Commissioner’s application for judicial review of the extension taken by DND and to go on to consider the validity of the extension of time asserted by DND

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Federal Court had jurisdiction to review DND's extension and its validity.

propositions.text: Commissioner seeks declaration for general guidance; DND's extension period was long but involved many documents and consultations
propositions.quote: The Commissioner in insisting on a declaration being issued is seeking nothing more than general guidance for future cases. Although the period taken by DND in this case appears long, a large number of documents was involved and extensive consultations were required

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Commissioner seeks guidance; DND's long extension involved many documents and consultations.

propositions.text: Institutions must demonstrate link between justification and extension length under paragraphs 9(1)(a) and (b)
propositions.quote: it is not enough for a government institution to simply assert the existence of a statutory justification for an extension and claim an extension of its choice. An effort must be made to demonstrate the link between the justification advanced and the length of the extension taken

paragraphs.summary: The court holds institutions must link justification to extension length under paragraphs 9(1)(a) and (b).

propositions.text: English and French texts of subsection 9(1) require extensions be reasonable or justified in circumstances
propositions.quote: Read together, what these two texts contemplate is that the extension be reasonable or justified in the circumstances

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 9(1) texts require extensions be reasonable or justified in the circumstances.

propositions.text: Extensions must show unreasonable interference with operations or impracticality of consultations to be valid
propositions.quote: a demonstration be made that unless the extension is taken, providing access will result in unreasonable or undue interference with the “operations of the government institution”... and that it is not reasonable, or practically possible, to expect that the necessary consultations can be completed

paragraphs.summary: The court states extensions must show undue interference or impractical consultations to be valid.

propositions.text: Institutions must rigorously assess and justify extension duration to pass reasonableness review
propositions.quote: a government institution confronted with a request involving a great number of documents and/or necessitating broad consultation must make a serious effort to assess the required duration, and that the estimated calculation be sufficiently rigorous, logic and supportable to pass muster under reasonableness review

paragraphs.summary: The court requires institutions to rigorously assess and justify extension duration for reasonableness.

propositions.text: DND's original formula for estimating extension time was logically deficient and failed to show genuine assessment
propositions.quote: DND originally claimed to have estimated the time taken... by simply dividing the number of pages requested by the number of pages involved in the average DFAIT consultation... this type of formula has on the face of it a deficient logic and falls short of demonstrating that a genuine attempt was made to assess the required duration

propositions.text: DND could not explain why other variables had no impact on the estimated time despite claiming they were considered
propositions.quote: Though DND later claimed that other variables were taken into account, it could not explain why... they had no impact whatsoever on the amount of time required under the formula disclosed in its original explanation

paragraphs.summary: The court finds DND's time estimate formula deficient and unexplained despite claimed consideration of other variables.

propositions.text: DND acted as though accountable only to itself in asserting its extension
propositions.quote: This type of perfunctory treatment of the matter shows that DND acted as though it was accountable to no one but itself in asserting its extension.

propositions.text: DND did not seriously assess the duration of the extension
propositions.quote: Its treatment of the matter falls short of establishing that a serious effort was made to assess the duration of the extension.

propositions.text: DND's extension does not meet subsection 9(1) requirements
propositions.quote: As such, the extension taken by DND does not meet the requirements of subsection 9(1).

propositions.text: Commissioner is entitled to the declaration sought
propositions.quote: This suffices to establish the Commissioner’s entitlement to the declaration sought.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds DND acted as if accountable only to itself, failed to seriously assess extension duration, did not meet subsection 9(1), so Commissioner is entitled to declaration.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed and judgment given that Federal Court judge should have given
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, I would allow the appeal and giving the judgment which the Federal Court judge should have given,

propositions.text: Declare DND entered deemed refusal state on March 5, 2011 after 30-day limit expired
propositions.quote: I would declare DND to have entered into a state of deemed refusal pursuant to subsection 10(3) of the Act on March 5, 2011, upon the expiration of the 30-day time limit set out in section 7 of the Act.

propositions.text: No costs awarded as none sought
propositions.quote: As no costs were sought, none are awarded.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, declares DND in deemed refusal on March 5, 2011, and awards no costs as none were sought.
